messages.content: Why does the Transformer use sinusoidal positional encodings rather than learned position embeddings?

The authors tried both learned positional embeddings and fixed sinusoidal encodings and found nearly identical results. They chose sinusoids because they might let the model extrapolate to sequence lengths longer than those seen during training, and they need no extra learned parameters.
How does multi-head attention keep its computational cost close to that of single-head attention?

Each head projects the queries, keys, and values to a smaller dimension, the model dimension divided by the number of heads, so the total cost of running all heads in parallel is similar to a single attention head at full dimensionality.
What is label smoothing and why did the Transformer authors use it?

Label smoothing replaces hard 0 or 1 training targets with slightly softened ones, with a value of 0.1 in the paper. It makes the model less over-confident, which hurts perplexity but improved accuracy and BLEU score.
Why is dot-product attention preferred over additive attention in the Transformer?

Dot-product attention is much faster and more space-efficient in practice because it can use highly optimized matrix multiplication code, even though the theoretical complexity is similar to additive attention. The scaling factor was added so that it also works well for large key dimensions.
Why is matrix B initialized to zero in LoRA while A is initialized randomly?

With B at zero, the product BA is zero at the start of training, so the adapted model begins exactly equal to the pretrained model. A random Gaussian initialization of A ensures the low-rank update can still receive useful gradients and learn from that starting point.
How does LoRA make it practical to serve many tasks from one base model?

Each task needs only its own small A and B matrices, while the large base weights are shared. Switching tasks means removing one task's update and adding another's, which is far cheaper than storing and loading a full fine-tuned copy of the model for every task.
How can RAG's knowledge be updated without retraining the model?

Because the knowledge lives in the external document index, you can replace or refresh the index with newer documents and the retriever will return updated passages. The paper demonstrated this by swapping the Wikipedia index for a different dump and seeing the answers change accordingly.
Why does RAG consider several retrieved documents instead of only the top one?

RAG treats the retrieved document as a latent variable and marginalizes over the top-K retrieved documents, so the output probability combines evidence from several passages. This makes it more robust when the single best-ranked passage is wrong or incomplete, and it lets gradients flow to the retriever.
Can RAG answer a question correctly when the answer is not literally present in the retrieved passages?

Sometimes, yes. Because it generates text rather than extracting a span, it can synthesize an answer from clues spread across retrieved documents or from its parametric knowledge, which an extractive reader cannot do.
How does retrieval-augmented generation differ from fine-tuning a model on the same documents?

Fine-tuning bakes the information into the model's weights, which makes it hard to update and to attribute. RAG keeps the documents in an external index that is searched at inference time, so knowledge can be updated by changing the index and answers can be traced to retrieved sources.
Why do prototypical networks use squared Euclidean distance rather than cosine distance?

Squared Euclidean distance is a Bregman divergence, which makes the class mean the right cluster representative, and the paper found it performed significantly better than cosine distance in practice.
How do prototypical networks relate to Matching Networks in the one-shot case?

With only one support example per class, the prototype is just that example's embedding, and the two methods become essentially equivalent. They differ with several shots, since prototypical networks average the examples while Matching Networks keep each support example separate.
Why is the simple design of prototypical networks considered an advantage for few-shot learning?

With very few labeled examples, models with extra parameters or complicated mechanisms tend to overfit. Prototypical networks use a simple inductive bias, one point per class and a fixed distance function, with no parameters beyond the embedding network, which the paper argues helps both efficiency and accuracy.
Why can a Matching Network classify classes it never saw in training without fine-tuning?

Classification is computed by attending over the labeled support set at test time, so a new class only requires placing its labeled examples in the support set. The learned embedding and attention mechanism generalize, so no gradient update is needed for new classes.
Why does weight-only quantization speed up LLM text generation?

Generation is dominated by memory bandwidth, since each generated token must read all the weights but does little arithmetic per byte. Storing weights in 3 to 4 bits shrinks memory traffic, giving speedups even though activations stay in higher precision. The paper reported roughly 3.25x on an A100 and 4.5x on an A6000 over FP16.
Are larger models more or less robust to GPTQ quantization than smaller ones?

Larger models are generally more robust: the accuracy gap to full precision shrinks as model size grows, so very large LLMs can be quantized to 3 or 4 bits with small loss while small models degrade more.
Why is quantization-aware training impractical for LLMs at the 100 billion parameter scale?

Quantization-aware training requires retraining the whole model with substantial data and compute, which is prohibitively expensive in memory and time at that scale. Post-training methods like GPTQ need only a small calibration set and a few GPU hours.
Roughly how much smaller are 4-bit quantized weights than FP16 weights?
FP16 uses 16 bits per weight and 4-bit quantization uses 4, so the weights take about four times less memory, slightly less than that once scales and other quantization metadata are counted.
How does GPTQ compare with simple round-to-nearest quantization at low bit widths?

Round-to-nearest degrades badly at 3 bits, particularly on large models, while GPTQ keeps accuracy much closer to full precision because it compensates for each rounding error using second-order information about the layer.
What precision scheme does SmoothQuant target, and why does it help hardware efficiency?

SmoothQuant targets W8A8, 8-bit weights and 8-bit activations. Using INT8 for both lets matrix multiplications run on INT8 kernels, giving up to about 1.56x speedup and 2x memory reduction with negligible accuracy loss.
What mathematical transformation does SmoothQuant apply to a linear layer?

It divides each input activation channel by a scale and multiplies the corresponding weight rows by the same scale, so the layer's output is mathematically unchanged in full precision. The per-channel scales balance the maximum activation and weight magnitudes, which makes both easier to quantize.
Why is the soft-target term multiplied by the temperature squared in distillation?

The gradients produced by the soft targets scale roughly as one over the temperature squared, so multiplying that term by T squared keeps the relative contribution of the soft and hard-label terms roughly unchanged when the temperature is varied.
What temperature does a distilled student use at deployment?
After training with a raised temperature, the student's temperature is set back to 1 at inference, so it produces ordinary softmax probabilities.
In knowledge distillation, what happens if the temperature is set very low?

At a very low temperature the softmax output approaches a one-hot distribution, so the soft targets look almost like hard labels. Little information about the relative probabilities of incorrect classes survives, and matching tends to ignore logits that are much more negative than average.
